title: Technical deep dive: Autoscaling & capacity planning
summary: Redwood SE-led deep dive on autoscaling strategy and capacity planning for Skyline Health Tech. Discussed reserved GPU pools vs burst policies, queueing/backpressure, batching and KV cache behavior at scale, quantization tradeoffs, and options for VPC/on-prem private deployment. Action items: benchmark plan, follow-up pricing for reserved pods, security docs for VPC private control plane.
topics: burst capacity and pre-warmed warm pools
quantization profiles impact on latency and memory
private/VPC deployment constraints and audit logs

Redwood to share dedicated pricing tiers for reserved GPUs and burst add-on (Jordan)
Customer to provide sample traffic profile and critical endpoints list (Tom)
Schedule on-prem feasibility call with infra team and security (Nora + Marco)
Set up trial tenant and run 72-hour warm pool test

transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2026-03-31; Start: 15:00 UTC; Duration: 60m; Attendees: Jordan, Priya, Marco (Redwood) — Aisha, Tom, Li, Nora (Skyline)
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining; we'll kick off, this is a deep dive on autoscaling & capacity planning for the inferencing layer, want to make sure we cover your latency sloa and cost constraints
[00:18] Aisha: yeah thanks Jordan, quick context — we run a mix of clinical note summarization and patient-facing chat, peaks during 8–10am and 6–8pm PST, target p95 latency for chat is 350ms, cost targets are really tight so we are evaluating dedicated reserved GPUs + burst on hosted for overflow
[00:35] Priya: great, that helps — one of the main tradeoffs is reserved capacity for predictable throughput vs using burst pools which can save money but adds variability; we typically recommend a hybrid: reserved for baseline throughput + burst for 2–3x peak events with queueing and graceful degradation
[00:52] Tom: can you expand on queueing? we worry about request pileup causing large latency spikes and dropped requests
[01:05] Priya: sure, so Redwood implements a few models: token-based queueing, per-customer concurrency limits, and weighted priority queues for critical endpoints. The queue length is bounded — we can configure soft and hard limits, and pre-specified fallback policies such as lower-capacity model variants or reroute to the hosted tier. At the runtime layer we also support backpressure signals to client SDKs so you can implement client-side exponential backoff
[01:42] Li: how does KV cache affect cold-starts and latency for chat? we rely heavily on long contexts and we want to avoid re-computing attention for repeated prefixes
[01:56] Marco: good question. KV cache affinity matters — when a request hits a different GPU instance without local KV warm-up you have to rebuild cache which adds ~50–150ms depending on sequence length. We expose cache warming features: sticky routing to keep sessions on same host, pre-warming cached prefixes on idle hosts, and shared remote KV stores for large-scale deployments though the network hop adds latency. For private/VPC we can locality-optimize the cache to reduce cross-host fetches
[02:28] Aisha: interesting, so for sessions we should prefer sticky routing, but what about autoscaling when you add nodes, won't that break stickiness?
[02:40] Priya: autoscaling has policy hooks — you can mark a host as 'draining' so it stops accepting new sessions while completing inflight requests, then we migrate or flush KV cache as needed. For scale-up we pre-warm new nodes with common prefixes if you provide representative prompt sets. That reduces the cold penalty significantly
[03:02] Tom: what's the warm-pool strategy — do you keep a small number of always-on GPUs in a warm state? and how expensive is that?
[03:16] Marco: yes, warm pools are a key pattern — keep N pre-warmed workers per region; cost depends on instance type and utilization. We recommend calculating baseline QPS and tail latency to pick N so you can absorb typical bursts without spinning up new GPUs under strict SLOs. The cost can be mitigated with smaller instance types for warm pools and autoscaling to larger instances for sustained load
[03:39] Li: can you talk about batching? we want to maximize throughput but maintain p95 latency at 350ms
[03:49] Priya: batching increases throughput by combining tokens across requests, but it adds waiting time — the batching policy is a dynamic threshold: max batch size and max wait window (e.g., 10ms/20ms). We also support latency-aware batching where requests near the SLO bypass batching or use a smaller batch window. For p95=350ms you can typically allow small batching windows (5–15ms) which gives good efficiency without breaking SLOs
[04:17] Aisha: what about quantization? we've heard that 8-bit quantization reduces memory and cost, but how does that affect latency and quality for our clinical models
[04:29] Marco: quantization reduces memory footprint and can increase throughput by enabling larger batch sizes per GPU, but there are tradeoffs: int8 can sometimes degrade quality on sensitive medical prompts. We recommend running a quantization validation on a representative eval set. For latency, quantized kernels are often faster for large sequences, but tiny sequences might not see wins. We usually provide quantization profiles and a recommended fallback pipeline (start with 16-bit for trials, move to 8-bit approx with calibration and eval thresholds)
[04:59] Nora: on security & VPC: we need private control plane, KMS integration, and SOC2/ISO type logs — do you support on-prem private deployments and audit log forwarding?
[05:12] Jordan: yes — Redwood Private supports a customer-managed control plane in a VPC, KMS/HSM key management, and audit log export. For on-prem installs we package the control plane and runtime; we can integrate with your SIEM and provide syslog/CloudWatch export. We'll share the security checklist after this call
[05:32] Tom: another concern: model fallbacks when capacity limited — we don't want to fail the whole app, prefer lower-capacity variant or cached response
[05:42] Priya: we have automated fallback chains — model variant table per endpoint that says: if GPU1 not available call model-B-quantized or model-C-hosted. Also prefix caching for deterministic responses can return cached outputs instantly. We surface fallbacks in tracing/metrics so you can track quality regressions
[06:05] Li: about reserved GPUs — how do we size reserved pools? we have 200 RPS baseline average, bursts to 800 RPS for 10–20 minutes during peaks, average token length 120 tokens per request
[06:19] Marco: quick calc: tokens/sec baseline = 200 * 120 = 24k tokens/s; you need to know tokens/s per GPU for your chosen model/quantization. If one GPU can do 6k tok/s at target latency with batching, you'd need ~4 reserved GPUs baseline; for bursts to 800 RPS you'd need 32k tok/s so reserve 6–7 GPUs and rely on burst to add another 2–3 instances, or increase reserved to match SLA. We'll provide a sizing spreadsheet. Important: batching efficiency and KV cache hit-rate can change these numbers a lot, so we'll calibrate with your traffic profile
[06:58] Aisha: can we do region-based capacity — patients are US east and west, want low latency in both regions
[07:08] Priya: yes, you can partition reserved capacity per region and use smart routing so user requests go to nearest region; cross-region fallback exists but we avoid it for latency-sensitive endpoints. For cost efficiency you can overprovision in one region and route non-critical background tasks to cheaper regions
[07:26] Tom: what's the cooldown/scale-down policy? we worry about thrash if it scales down too fast after a brief dip
[07:37] Marco: cooldown timers and stable-window metrics — we typically recommend a longer cooldown for scale-down (5–15 minutes) and shorter scale-up (30–90s) with multiple metrics (CPU/GPU utilization, queue length, token lag). This avoids thrash. You can also set minimum replica counts (min reserved) so you never scale below a safe baseline
[07:57] Nora: for on-prem — network egress/ingress and KV store placement: we can't have external shared KV stores leaving the VPC, what are options?
[08:10] Priya: we support local persistent KV shards per cluster and a synchronous replication option inside the VPC. Alternatively, you can use an in-cluster distributed cache (e.g., Redis) managed by you. We do not require external internet access for cache traffic in Private deployments
[08:26] Li: any recommendations for tooling to monitor capacity and predict bursts? we'd like to automate alerts that recommend pre-warm actions
[08:36] Jordan: Redwood Console exposes per-route token-level metrics, predicted tail latency, and suggested autoscale actions. For forecasting we can integrate with your historical metrics and output suggested warm-pool sizes and time windows for scheduled warm-ups — we'll include a sample forecast in the benchmark plan
[08:55] Aisha: on cost modelling, curious about how batching improves unit cost and how that maps to reserved vs burst pricing
[09:03] Marco: batching improves tokens-per-GPU efficiency which lowers unit cost. Reserved pricing gives lower unit price but you pay for idle time. Burst pricing is higher per-token but avoids commit. We provide an Optimize tool that simulates costs across different batch sizes, quantization, and warm-pool sizes using your traffic profile
[09:20] Tom: i want to run an initial benchmark — what's the recommended test: steady-state and spike tests?
[09:27] Priya: recommend 3 tests: 1) steady-state at baseline QPS for 30–60m, 2) spike test: ramp from baseline to peak in 5 minutes and hold for 15–30m, 3) cold-start test with scale from zero to peak repeated 5 times. Capture p50/p95/p99 latencies, tokens/sec, batch sizes, and KV hit rates. We'll provide the harness and config
[09:50] Li: any pitfalls around quantized models and batch sizing? sometimes we saw reduced quality at high batch sizes
[09:58] Marco: yes, quality regressions can happen; the eval harness should check generation metrics and domain-specific scoring (e.g., medical correctness). Also note that some ops have non-linear perf with batch size — test a range of batch sizes (8, 16, 32)
[10:12] Jordan: quick recap: Redwood will send benchmark plan + harness, pricing for reserved pods and burst add-on, security checklist for VPC/private, and a sizing spreadsheet. Skyline to send traffic histograms and schedule on-prem feasibility call. We'll target trial tenant setup next week
[10:29] Aisha: sounds good, thanks everyone
[10:34] Tom: thanks, bye

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings and filler words preserved; some product names spelled variably (KV cache, kv-cache, K/V).
